solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: City areas less urban, on reflection? Not entirely

indicators.note: a mirror reflection shows things back to front, so the letters are read right to left
only part of the phrase is used, so the answer lies inside it rather than using all of it

parts.note: the letters run across the words: areaS LESS URBan

explanation.surface: A musing on whether some parts of a city feel less urban than others.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'Not entirely' make it look like a remark about suburbs; the answer is lying backwards across the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Belgian capital is one of countless cities.

clue.text: Newly organised soldiers also took charge

explanation.surface: Soldiers being reorganised while also taking command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newly organised' looks like an anagram indicator for 'soldiers', but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: a factory re-equipped with new tools is set up afresh, so the word stretches to any reorganisation.

clue.text: Direct approach secures answer immediately

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so the outer phrase closes round the letter

parts.note: a straight way = a direct approach
A = answer, as in Q and A

explanation.surface: Advice that a direct approach gets you an answer at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direct approach' reads as a single idea in the surface, and it really does supply the outside of the answer, split by A.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean without any delay.

clue.text: Fatigue rising about heartless African from part of Africa

indicators.note: in a down clue, something rising goes upward, so the word is read from the bottom up
with the heart, the middle, cut out, only the two ends of the word are left

parts.note: AFRICAN with its inside removed leaves A…N

explanation.surface: A tired African traveller from somewhere in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Eritrea is a country on the Red Sea coast in the Horn of Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective of origin: the Horn of Africa country Eritrea is the part of Africa meant.

clue.text: Unseemly argument, perhaps over railway setting?

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed over another sits above it in the column

parts.note: making a scene: a public row is one example

explanation.surface: A row that broke out over a railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' flags that an unseemly argument is only one kind of scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre sense: the painted backdrop on stage provides a play's setting.

clue.text: Gym apparatus? Lands with head lowered

indicators.note: the head of a down word is its top letter, and lowering it moves that letter further down the column

explanation.surface: A gymnast landing head down on the apparatus.
explanation.walkthrough: The S at the top of SHORES drops down to become the fourth letter; the question mark admits that 'apparatus' has to be read as plural.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: vaulting and pommel horses are two items of gym apparatus.

clue.text: Author has to support good play

indicators.note: in a down clue, whatever supports something is placed beneath it

parts.note: the setter is the author, and 'I have' is written I'VE

explanation.surface: A writer backing a good stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' is not a drama but slack, the looseness in a rope or a steering wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of slack: a rope with some give has some play in it.

clue.text: Right hand agitated my itch connected with pulse?

indicators.note: something agitated is stirred up and shaken, so the letters lose their order

explanation.surface: A twitchy right hand, with an itch that throbs with the pulse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' suggests the heartbeat, but here it is a musical beat.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical sense: a pulse is a regular beat, and music with one has rhythm.

clue.text: Rather stupid, introducing bit of lamb into fish course

indicators.note: only a small bit of the word is taken, its first letter
the letter goes into the phrase that follows

parts.note: a cod dish is a fish course

indicators.note: to introduce something is to bring it in, so the letter is put inside

explanation.surface: A daft chef adding lamb to the fish course.
explanation.walkthrough: The L slots in straight after the C of COD DISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Built from a noun: a clod is a dolt, and -ish makes it 'rather' so.

clue.text: Backed disturbances, but not over prison

indicators.note: something backed has been moved backwards, so the word is read right to left
'not' excludes what comes next, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: O = over, in cricket scoring; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: Supporting prison riots, though not one over the prison itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone backing a riot; dropping the O from the reversed word is what matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Old criminal slang: to be 'in stir' is to be in prison.

clue.text: Shock? The man isn't so shocked

indicators.note: a shocked thing is jolted out of place, so the letters are jolted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone asks if something is a shock, and a man replies he isn't so shocked.
explanation.walkthrough: Definition and indicator are the same word in two forms, which makes the clue feel like a conversation rather than a recipe.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: great surprise is a kind of shock, which the question mark allows.

clue.text: Having a reasonable salary suggests open-minded management primarily?

parts.note: a playful hint: managers who take a moderate, middle-ground view, holding a central position in the pay scale

explanation.surface: A query about whether broad-minded bosses earn a decent wage.
explanation.walkthrough: The second part is a whimsical hint rather than strict wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Middle-income households earn neither a lot nor a little, an adequate wage in the central band.

clue.text: Badger turned up around trail beside rear of pasture

indicators.note: the last piece sits next to the rest
the reversed word goes round the next one
turned means flipped round, so the little word is read backwards

parts.note: to lag is to trail behind

indicators.note: the rear is the back end, so the last letter of the field word

explanation.surface: A badger surfaces near a track at the back of a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badger' looks like the animal in a country scene, but it is the verb meaning pester.
explanation.definitionFit: To badger someone is to pester them persistently, which is the verb sense of plague.

clue.text: What remains strange about side playing United?

indicators.note: one thing about another goes round it, so the outer word encloses the rest
things at play move about freely, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: U = United, as in football team names

explanation.surface: A strange question about a team playing against United.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Side' and 'United' look like two football teams in a fixture; both feed the same anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical synonym: residuum is the Latin-derived word for a residue, what is left over.

clue.text: French writer recalled receiving money for working on newspaper?

indicators.note: something recalled is called back, so the name is read backwards
a word receiving another takes it inside itself

explanation.surface: A French author paid for journalism, recalled years later.
explanation.walkthrough: Gide was a French novelist; the question mark admits that editing is only one way to work on a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: editing is one of the jobs done on a newspaper.

clue.text: Hour after the Spanish occasion is a late one

indicators.note: the piece named first comes after the others in the answer

explanation.surface: A Spanish party that does not get going until the small hours.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on 'the eleventh hour', the last possible moment.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the eleventh hour is proverbially a late one, just before time runs out.

clue.text: Spineless individual, American, about to follow associate of Capone?

indicators.note: these pieces follow, coming after the gangster's companion

explanation.surface: A cowardly American hanging around after one of Al Capone's gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spineless' reads as cowardly, but the answer literally has no backbone.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal reading: molluscs are invertebrates, creatures with no spine at all.

clue.text: Rock face banning English, one in Scottish town

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the town's name

parts.note: Oban is a port town on the west coast of Scotland

indicators.note: banning means excluding, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: a side is a face, as of a cube
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A rock face where the English are banned, and someone in a Scottish town.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsidian is a dark volcanic glass formed when lava cools fast, a type of igneous stone.

clue.text: Film star's horse in pride of place here?

definitions.text: horse in pride of place here?
definitions.meaning: a cryptic hint: where the top horse would be stabled

explanation.surface: A film star's prized racehorse kept in the best stable.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as STALL ONE, the number one stall, which is where a horse in pride of place would be kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Sylvester Stallone, of Rocky and Rambo, is a Hollywood film star.

clue.text: Snake here has more than half twisted

indicators.note: four of the seven letters at the front of the word are turned back to front

parts.note: to be present is to be here

explanation.surface: A snake is here, with most of its body coiled up.
explanation.walkthrough: Reverse the first four letters of PRESENT, PRES, to give SERP, and keep ENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A serpent is a literary word for a snake, especially a large one.

clue.text: Decline farewell involving capital of Wales or place nearby?

indicators.note: the two words take in a letter between them

parts.note: to ebb is to decline or recede

indicators.note: the capital is the first letter

explanation.surface: A departing farewell that wraps in the Welsh capital or somewhere close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital of Wales' looks like Cardiff, but it is just W. Ebbw Vale is a town in South Wales, not far from Cardiff.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebbw Vale is a Welsh town near Cardiff, so a locality in the vicinity of the capital.

clue.text: Impassioned sporting body elevated game

indicators.note: in a down entry, elevated means raised, so the letters read upwards

parts.note: the FA is the Football Association
game means lame, as in a game leg

explanation.surface: A football association promotes a sport with real passion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like a sport, but it is the adjective: a game leg is a lame one. The FA is English football's governing body.
explanation.definitionFit: Aflame is figurative for burning with strong feeling or passion.

clue.text: I run in circuits, going round curving course

indicators.note: the reversed word goes round the others, enclosing them

explanation.surface: A runner going round and round a winding track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circuits' does double duty in the surface as laps of the track, and that is exactly what it gives before being turned.
explanation.definitionFit: A shape word: a path that keeps winding round a centre follows a spiral.

clue.text: Enclosed line in revised copy — editor in charge covering everything

parts.note: ENC is the abbreviation for enclosed on a letter

indicators.note: the line is placed in the middle of the reworked copy
revised copy is copy rewritten, so its letters change order

explanation.surface: An editor tells an assistant to insert a line into a revised draft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enclosed' looks like the container signal, but it is the abbreviation written at the foot of a letter; 'in' does the enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Encyclopedic knowledge is comprehensive, taking in every subject.

clue.text: Pitch marker almost split

indicators.note: almost all of the word, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: cleft = split, less its final T

explanation.surface: A marker on a sports pitch that has nearly split.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' suggests a sports field, but it is musical pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical sense: the sign at the start of a stave marks which pitch each line stands for.

clue.text: Wind player ducks end of piece after interruption of 'Bravo'

indicators.note: an interruption breaks into the middle, so the letter goes between the two Os
the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so two ducks are O and O
Bravo is B in the NATO alphabet

indicators.note: the last letter of the word it picks from

explanation.surface: A wind player ducking out of the end of a piece as the audience shouts bravo.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the instrument, but orchestras also call the player by the instrument's name, as in 'second oboe'.
explanation.definitionFit: A metonymy: in an orchestra a player is named for the instrument, so the second oboe is a person.

clue.text: The control securing source of music in electronic instrument

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it safely inside, so the rein closes round the letter

parts.note: the + rein, a control on a horse

indicators.note: the source of something is where it begins, so the first letter

explanation.surface: A control on an electronic instrument that gets the music going.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is famously played without touch, the hands moving near two antennae, which makes 'control' a nice touch.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Russian-invented theremin was among the first electronic instruments.

clue.text: Contract returned before finale from star fiddler

indicators.note: something returned is sent back, so the word is read right to left

parts.note: to knit is to contract, draw together, as brows do; KNIT turned round

indicators.note: the finale is the ending, so the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A star violinist's contract, renewed just before the final concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddler' and 'star' suggest a violinist; the fiddler here is someone who fiddles with gadgets.
explanation.definitionFit: A second sense of fiddle: to fiddle about with a machine is to tinker with it.
